problems.issue: The defining sodium-losing enteropathy is largely absent beyond the label 'secretory diarrhea': elevated fecal sodium and villous atrophy are absent, while elevated fecal pH, metabolic acidosis, hyponatremia and intractable diarrhea occur in only 1–3%. All were reported in every R1-train patient. Reporting loss cannot explain these near-zero TRUE rates. This would teach an inadequately severe and biochemically nonspecific disease phenotype.

Associated hallmark findings are underrepresented: choanal atresia is reported in 20%, versus bilateral choanal atresia in 56% of R1-train patients; corneal erosion is reported in 21% including specific terms, versus 56%. Broader choanal terminology partly explains the bilateral-term discrepancy, but not the overall shortfall.

Optic disc coloboma, cutis laxa, urinary tract duplication and macrocephaly receive disproportionate emphasis relative to the defining intestinal findings. Example 1 is crowded with nonspecific craniofacial and ear findings, and example 2 provides little indication of severe congenital sodium-losing diarrhea.

summary: Secretory diarrhea and several characteristic congenital anomalies are represented, but the profound loss of the defining intestinal and biochemical phenotype makes these patients implausible. Sex balance and median age are not independently concerning; age at ascertainment need not equal congenital onset.
